opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that these two communities have historically worked in very separate silos, even though the choices each one makes deeply constrain the other. Hardware is designed on very long cycles. You're often making bets years in advance about what workloads will matter. Meanwhile, algorithm developers tend to treat the hardware as fixed, almost a given, and they gravitate toward ideas that happen to run well on whatever's available. That's the dynamic I've described as the hardware lottery: an idea often succeeds not because it's universally superior, but because it fits the existing software and hardware stack.

Software portability sits in the middle. When you look at how well a framework lets an operation move from one type of hardware to another, you quickly see how much friction there is. Some operations run beautifully on one accelerator and are painfully slow, or don't work at all, on another. That friction quietly shapes which research directions people pursue. If you're a researcher and your idea is ten times slower to try, you're probably going to abandon it, even if it might have been the better path.

So a common language matters because, without it, neither side can really see the cost of its decisions on the other. Hardware architects need to understand which algorithmic directions are being prematurely closed off. Algorithm developers need to understand that what feels like a fundamental property of a method is sometimes just an artifact of tooling. If we can measure and talk about portability in shared terms, like what breaks, what slows down, and where the gaps are, it becomes much easier to co-design and to keep the space of ideas open, rather than letting the current stack dictate what we explore next.

For me, it's ultimately about scientific progress. I don't want the next breakthrough to be lost simply because it lost the lottery.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that right now these two communities barely talk to each other, and that's not because of a lack of goodwill, it's because they don't have a shared vocabulary. If you're a hardware architect, you're thinking in terms of memory bandwidth, data movement, how much parallelism you can expose, what kind of precision the arithmetic units support. If you're an algorithm developer, you're thinking about a loss landscape, about convergence, about whether your idea works on a benchmark. And the thing that connects those two worlds, which is really the software stack and the compiler layer, has mostly been treated as plumbing that nobody wants to own.

The consequence of that is what I've called the hardware lottery. Ideas don't succeed purely on their merits, they succeed partly because they happen to map well onto the hardware and software that already exists. Deep learning itself is the obvious example, right? The core ideas were around for decades, and they only took off once GPUs, which were built for a totally different purpose, turned out to be a good fit for matrix multiplies. So when I think about portability, I'm not just thinking about the engineering convenience of running the same model on different chips. I'm thinking about whether the next good idea that doesn't look like a dense matmul gets a fair hearing.

And for that to happen, the algorithm person needs to be able to express what their method actually requires, sparse access patterns, irregular compute, whatever it is, in a way the hardware person can reason about, and the hardware person needs to be able to communicate the real costs and constraints back, without each side having to become an expert in the other's field. That's what I mean by a common language. It's partly abstractions, partly tooling, but it's also just culturally agreeing that this interface is a first class research problem. Because if we don't build it, we keep narrowing the space of ideas we're willing to explore, and we won't even notice we're doing it.

r004.rationale: It says algorithm developers should be able to express what their methods require, such as sparse or irregular computation, so hardware architects can reason about it, without either side needing expertise in the other’s field.

astra-6.text:
Because the choices we make on the algorithm side and the choices we make on the hardware side are deeply connected, but those communities often work with very different assumptions. An algorithm developer might say, “I’ve reduced the number of operations, so this should be faster.” But a hardware architect knows that speed also depends on things like memory movement and whether the hardware can actually take advantage of that reduction.

Sparsity is a useful example. Having fewer nonzero weights doesn’t automatically translate into lower latency. You need support across the software and hardware stack to turn that theoretical saving into a practical benefit.

So a common language lets us communicate what an algorithm needs and what a particular platform makes efficient. For me, portability is partly about making those dependencies clearer, so that exploring a new idea doesn’t require every researcher to become an expert in every hardware platform.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the decisions those two groups make are deeply connected, but they often don’t have much visibility into each other’s constraints. As an algorithm developer, you might think about the number of operations in your model, or how many parameters it has. But those measures don’t necessarily tell you how fast it will run on a particular piece of hardware. Moving data around can matter enormously, and so can whether the hardware actually supports the operations you’re using efficiently.

Sparsity is a good example. You can remove a lot of weights from a network, but that doesn’t automatically translate into a speedup. The hardware and the software stack have to be able to take advantage of that structure.

So I see portability as a way of making those dependencies visible. We need a shared language for describing what an algorithm needs and what a hardware platform can deliver. That lets algorithm developers make more informed choices, and it gives hardware architects a better understanding of which capabilities would actually enable new ideas.
